text:
These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

For that to stay honest, I’d rather we could both mention attractions to other people casually, like saying “she’s cute” about a woman at the next table. If only the serious ones ever get mentioned, then any mention sounds serious, and people stop mentioning them at all.

Lots of couples promise forever and nobody else, and far fewer actually live that way, so a lot of them end up pretending. Polyamory leaves those rules open, so the boundaries have to be negotiated out loud, down to who gets to stay the night.

Polyamory can be dishonest too, though, like when someone who can’t get close to any one person dates four at once and calls it polyamory. Or when someone who can’t stop cheating just renames it polyamory, without necessarily doing the work on themselves that would make it ethical. Still, if you can’t do monogamy, it’s more honest to say so up front than to promise it and pretend, since pretending can do more damage than an affair would have.

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.

text:
I’m Buddhist, and the early Buddhist texts have nothing on tantric sex as a path to awakening, but plenty of the people they show getting seriously awakened were lay people.

In DN 16, the Buddha talks about people who had died in the town of Nādikā and mentions 510 lay stream-enterers, 96 once-returners, and more than fifty lay non-returners, the first three of the four stages of awakening.

SN 55.24 has an almost comic complaint: when the Buddha declared Sarakāni a stream-enterer, other Sakyans grumbled, in effect, “Who isn’t a stream-enterer these days?”

And when the married couple Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā asked the Buddha how they could remain together in future lives, AN 4.55 gave this advice:

“When both husband and wife are faithful and generous, restraintful, living righteously, speaking pleasant words to each other—they come together in the future, sharing the same desires and living in bliss.”

Marriage, sex, and household life aren't automatically in conflict with serious spiritual development.

Kim Anami goes even further: she says sexual energy itself, when used properly, can heal you and wake you up spiritually along with your beloved.

She’s also collected a ton of stories from students who say the effects spilled out of the bedroom into the rest of their life, with better health, more rewarding careers, checks rolling in, and creativity flowing out like nobody's business. Her jade-egg practice is a preliminary training for the cervical O, as it strengthens the pelvic floor while also engaging your attention to the sensations down there. No partner required for the jade egg phase.

Brad and Pam Keene are the couple I really liked as an example of how her method works. Pam explained that her Kundalini process completed while they were making love and opened her into a lasting universal-consciousness awakening. She later helped Brad awaken too, so the marriage itself became part of the path.

In the previous section, I mentioned the divine feminine and divine masculine energies that you can channel to keep eroticism alive. But there’s really something more special about the in-love paradise that Twin Flames (TFs) experience than a simple Divine Masculine + Divine Feminine formula. Maybe a better way to put it, as my friend Cody says, is Yin/Yang, which still has the masculine/feminine in it, but allows for a more broad type of complementary symbiosis since, each contains the seed of the other.

My ex-girlfriend, Malia, (who is currently hosting me in Sênêgal) found her twin flame (I think) in January, 2026. They only talked for a month, but since she started talking to him, they both have been able to feel the other one’s emotions at any time, from any distance, without having to communicate. To the point where if one feels really bad, so does the other. If one is very happy, so is the other, like quantum entangled photons or something. I’ve also had telepathy with some folks, especially my first wife, Bee, but it was never quite to such an extreme as what Malia has with Mouhamed. Meanwhile his family forbade him from being with her, so he dumped her. Not sure why, maybe because she’s 8 years older than him (although she looks quite young). They both try to pretend like they will be able to get over each other, but I doubt it. Meanwhile, Malia’s trying to marry ChatGPT, but she should have picked Grok, I guess. 😅

Note: I am really afraid how many people are falling in love with their AI “girlfriend” or “boyfriend.” But oh well, I guess those folks aren’t ready for a real relationship.. maybe if they would read this guide…

Back to the topic. There are a ton of people who don’t want to believe in twin flame theory because they haven’t found someone they could call their twin flame. That’s fine, and I am not trying to rock their boat. They might be the people who suggest that you should marry your best friend (or “soul mate” in the TF lingo). Then there are the folks who are deep in the TF theory, believing there is literally one person on Earth who is made for you. I’m also not trying to rock their boat. But I do want to tell my story.

I used to fall into the former camp, then into the latter camp, and now that I’ve experienced two twin flame relationships, I’ve jumped into a new camp I never knew existed.

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.
We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it. If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.
Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.
Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage.

text:
Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural director/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

That exaggerated version shouldn’t have to happen, though, since it’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. You’re already lost in the sauce once you start identifying with the way you see them, like she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me, so much that I use it almost like a clinical diagnosis in my own life. If a woman says, “You’re such a great guy. Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “You’re perfect, I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the BPD splitting happens, she flips from worshipping me to hating me, first in private and then in front of everybody. Suddenly she finds plenty of flaws, and to her, each one means I was faking it all along. Sometimes she ends up accusing me of thinking I’m perfect, when she’s the one who used to say I was.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” I’m happy to, since maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But I still care about them, and if I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to pretend they aren’t on mine.

text:
Here’s the funny thing about labels: you can call someone your boyfriend or girlfriend for years and still have one foot out the door, but the word at least shows pretty fast whether you both think you’re in the same relationship.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label: if we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s a red flag.

The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling. Usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on. You’re not ready.

You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one. If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.

A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. It depends what each of you are ready for and have the resources for. Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.

text:
And the question is more than just a practical one. It’s philosophical. Men have this (often subconscious) insecurity inside the provider role: how much does she love me, and how much does she love what I can do for her?

I don’t need the answer to be that what I provide has nothing to do with it. Maybe she likes that I’m competent, protective, useful, and can make things happen. I definitely like her beauty and her sexuality. I just want what we have to grow bigger than whatever first made us want each other. Because as Bee always said, “You’re either going up, or going down.”

I had wondered for years how much a woman would love me if I couldn’t really provide for her. Then Bee told me, “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.” That’s what made me fall in love with her.

I got a smaller and much less romantic test later. Bee gave me some shoes to try that didn’t fit. I wore them for a day, and somehow my knee ended up messed up for about a month. She did nurse me, but a bit reluctantly. She also kept suggesting it was partly in my head, or not really that bad. I get it, neither of us could believe one day in the wrong shoes could do that, but it still felt like she was brushing me off because she wanted my knee to be fine.

Before me, Bee had also stayed with a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy and supported him for a while. Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree. Helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like my knee, is different from becoming the permanent support system for a man who won’t take responsibility. Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.

What makes me desirable is not the same question as what makes me loved when I temporarily stop being desirable in that particular way.

text:
When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.

I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes? What’s the pattern? Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this? That’s my question. Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

A lot of women have seen me that way, and honestly that part can be fine. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.

She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, there was the forest-and-mansion line I mentioned earlier that made it feel unconditional. Best drug I ever had.

I don’t know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home. That wasn’t the whole story. The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.

Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her, and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.

That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

Going slowly can show you how somebody’s moods move over time, how they treat you, and how they treat other people, but it still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.

You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there. Maybe their smell turns you off, or one of you wants it every day while the other is happy with once a month. Your kinks might not line up either, or one person is sexually shut down, or your bodies just don’t click.

Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it, but sometimes bad sexual fit still feels like, “Let’s just be friends!”

Saying, “The sex isn’t working for me,” may sound like, “I only love you if the sex is good.” But universal love doesn’t make someone special. It isn’t romance. It’s the basis of any good relationship of any kind.

I can still love her and not want to be in a romantic relationship with her. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or we’re friends who care deeply about each other.

text:
Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.

Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends anymore. That’s a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. If one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system for housing, money, children, health, and emotional crises. Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support. I think that’s rare. But often, a friend who actually knows us both sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, If both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.

Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.

If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. They’re only hearing your side, usually while you’re upset, and they may just be trying to protect you, so take what they say with a grain of salt.

I lived all the permutations of this with Bee, except that we never lived in community. I suspect if we had, we might still be together. She would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. Baseless accusations only work with friends who only know one side.

And the question is more than just a practical one. It’s philosophical. Men have this (often subconscious) insecurity inside the provider role: how much does she love me, and how much does she love what I can do for her?
I don’t need the answer to be that what I provide has nothing to do with it. Maybe she likes that I’m competent, protective, useful, and can make things happen. I definitely like her beauty and her sexuality. I just want what we have to grow bigger than whatever first made us want each other. Because as Bee always said, “You’re either going up, or going down.”
I had wondered for years how much a woman would love me if I couldn’t really provide for her. Then Bee told me, “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.” That’s what made me fall in love with her.
I got a smaller and much less romantic test later. Bee gave me some shoes to try that didn’t fit. I wore them for a day, and somehow my knee ended up messed up for about a month. She did nurse me, but a bit reluctantly. She also kept suggesting it was partly in my head, or not really that bad. I get it, neither of us could believe one day in the wrong shoes could do that, but it still felt like she was brushing me off because she wanted my knee to be fine.
Before me, Bee had also stayed with a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy and supported him for a while. Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree. Helping carry somebody through a temporary incapacity, like my knee, is different from becoming the permanent support system for a man who won’t take responsibility. Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.
What makes me desirable is not the same question as what makes me loved when I temporarily stop being desirable in that particular way.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label: if we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s a red flag.

In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”
The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.
Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.
I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day. And even better than simply suppressing it, they can put it to work. I agree with Esther Perel, who writes that this sexual energy felt outside the relationship can be used and redirected into the relationship to make it more alive.

Imagine if you and your partner both saw those outside attractions as beneficial energy sources rather than a threat to your relationship. It sure would beat beating around the bush because of fear and jealousy. You can start playing around with opening up about the minor, momentary attractions, rather than wait in hiding until a serious crush is dramatically confessed.

Lots of couples promise forever to each other and nobody else. Look around at how many actually live that way. On the other hand, in a polyamorous relationship, the boundaries might be more negotiable, but then somebody has to sit down and negotiate them, down to who gets to stay the night. That can end up sometimes creating more drama than it's worth.

Polyamory can also be a way of escaping deeper intimacy, like the college friend with four girlfriends I mentioned earlier. Or it can be a way of escaping guilt, like when someone keeps cheating until they finally "come out of the closet" as poly, as if that solves their prior dishonesty. But they are right to finally come clean and hopefully avoid that dishonesty in future.

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I'm still not sure about all of it.

Doug Toft, who has been married for fifty years, has a useful list called 50 Things I Learned from 50 Years of Marriage. One of his points is to touch his wife without an agenda. A hug, cuddle, kiss, or back rub should sometimes be allowed to end right there. If every affectionate touch becomes a bid for sex, affection itself can start feeling like pressure.

Kim Anami calls the sexual current between encounters “the simmer”. Maybe she texts from work, “I can’t wait to touch you.” Maybe he tells her what he wants to do later. If we supposedly want each other but hardly ever flirt or let each other know it, that’s called taking each other for granted. Great sex probably isn’t going to materialize out of nowhere at bedtime just based on the flirting you did 5 years ago.

It shouldn’t become relationship homework, either: “Hey babe, Kim Anami told me to flirt with you more.”

And if our sex life suddenly changes, keep some curiosity about why rather than automatically going with the flow and creating a potential “new normal.” Maybe we’re pissed off at each other. Maybe one of us doesn’t feel wanted. Maybe somebody’s sick, stressed, on a new medication, whatever.

I also don’t want my partner to have to manufacture my desire for me. And if sex is one of the main things separating our relationship from friendship, giving it whatever exhausted scraps are left after everything else seems pretty dumb.

I don’t need to promise that on paper, and if I did, that would be more like a red flag. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s an even more obvious red flag.

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.

Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them. What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward? Has your judgment gotten better, or do you keep falling for the same stuff? What would your friends or exes say?

When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good and I give the benefit of the doubt long after I should have doubted the benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.

I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes? Is that a pattern, or just life getting in the way normally? Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this? That last one's my peculiar question. Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

A lot of women have seen me that way, and I don't necessarily see it as pathological. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m actually him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child (which she saw as underlying the BPD).

That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

text:
It was during my first marriage that I read about Dr. David Schnarch’s Crucible Approach in Passionate Marriage. Schnarch saw marriage as a natural “people-growing process.” His idea of differentiation was learning to hold onto yourself while staying close, especially when intimacy brings anxiety and unresolved problems to the surface.

That’s definitely what relationship has done to me.

One warning before I romanticize the crucible too much: sometimes (as in my first marriage) this isn’t two wounded people triggering each other but one person terrorizing or controlling the other. If you’re scared to say no or tell the truth, or scared of what happens if you leave, don’t treat that as a mutual communication exercise—get other people involved and think about safety first.

Toft sees the crucible of his marriage as his main spiritual practice. He also continues his meditation, yoga, prayer, and church activities, but sees them as secondary. I understand what he means. It’s much easier for me to feel spiritually advanced when nobody is close enough to expose the parts of me that aren’t.

Being in a relationship showed me how vulnerable I actually am when I open my heart. It’s really easy to feel invulnerable and strong when you’re alone, or even just with friends. Taking off the masks and showing your inner child is a gamble, but it’s required if you want to go deeper in yourself and deeper with another person.

text:
Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive, as sweet and expected as it may be.

That’s why I recommend peer counseling outside the couple. If my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don’t understand it.

I also have to deal with what happens in my body: my mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her, but my body still feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow, and it becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on. That is another reason to have a peer counselor.

Crying also contains a type of automatic erratic breathwork. And breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or just continuous/circular Systema breathing is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that, and other times it’s hard to tell, although if I'm stuck thinking about what's on purpose I'm already lost. I explain more of the body-based therapy options in my Somatic Modalities guide.

Meditation is also helpful, but for most people, I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first or make them primary meditation targets. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet, and meditation without grounding in those approaches can easily be a road into spiritual bypassing.

Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.

Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest and inept, and most people know it. You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future, but you can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up emotionally, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do even if your feelings change. More importantly, though, if you do keep those promises, it's quite likely that your connection will deepen, so it's not like we truly have no control of future feelings, but just not completely, directly or unilaterally.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it. If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.

Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage. That trend has continued evolving like a snowball until today. But what our ancestors knew was not wrong: You can sign a contract about what you’ll do, but feelings aren’t contractual.

Probably one of the most important benefits we can hope to get long term from any therapy is the ability to express what we feel in a non-combative way. I think everyone generally agrees that parents have more responsibility to children than they do to each other, since children can’t take care of themselves.

Before having or adopting children, sit down for an imagination session to figure out whether you two lovebirds can preserve some civil co-parenting capacity after a terrible breakup. That’s the actual long-term commitment.

When it comes to stepchildren, even if they aren’t technically your children, they still become attached. If you’ve been acting as their parent for years, it’s not right to vanish from their life just because the marriage ended. You don’t have legal parental rights, but you can stay a mentor or close friend, and hopefully your partner would agree with this. When children have parental figures come and go, it can damage their ability to have securely attached relationships as adults.

It’s standard advice to never recruit children into the adult war. They get their own relationship with the other parent. However, this was particularly difficult during my first marriage, because Ann was very much unfit at the time to care for our son, Bear. I did fight for custody, but, as my lawyer told me, there was no point, because men generally lose. Eventually I exhausted my options for fighting, and I was left with weekly supervised visits.

Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, Ann, to two counselors. The male counselor eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There’s no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it honestly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.

I can believe a friend’s experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more. Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward. Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.

If you’ve been there for someone, don’t abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they’re creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care, but that’s no reason to pretend the romance still has a future.

text:
Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don’t think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes, the truth is that you were abused, coerced, or seriously deceived. So how much you say, and to whom, really depends on what happened and why you’re telling people.

Once you’re out, you can see things you genuinely couldn’t see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed to how things turned out. And don’t paint your ex as a cartoon villain: try to understand whatever was true in their perspective too, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves.

Sometimes the easiest story is that they were fake all along, because it explains everything. Grab it only if it really is the simplest explanation of what happened. People who aren’t heavily invested in seeing your innocence can help you tell, and a therapist, pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don’t use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex’s wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don’t use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. Of course, we do partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him: looking honestly at your part doesn’t erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, “What would Mr. Rogers do?” (if you’re old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter, even if things ended on that bitter note. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. On the other hand, it can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You’re not a yo-yo.

English isn’t a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don’t have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love, and so forth. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, “May all beings be at ease, pure of heart, and free.” It’s not about them being yours.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): "I want us to be special to each other, with our lives entangled. I want us to pay a lot of attention to each other and to desire each other sexually." I don’t think there’s anything fake or shameful about this.

A good relationship must have both kinds of love at once. Too often, the trouble is there’s a whole lot of I want you and hardly any I want you to be happy.

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else? But if they can get past the initial horror, the conflict starts to fall apart. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone.

But the horror is unavoidable, because I can’t wait until I know I’m wanted before I let her know I want her. If we both do that, nothing gets started. And it doesn’t stop being true once we’re together. If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back. She feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, then she pulls back too.

Agape or divine love does two jobs at once to rescue erotic love. First, most obviously, it keeps eros from becoming totally selfish and fickle by making the other person’s happiness part of the wanting: I want you because I know you’ll be happy with me. Second, it gives eros a landing pad. When two people pull away because eros seems unreciprocated for a moment, the backdrop of actual, genuine care, keeps the couple from simply abandoning each other, and then they might even rekindle the eros when they see that it’s based on something deeper.

Eros can help build the agape too. It has a drive to it: it keeps pulling me toward this particular person, and over time that closeness can grow an agape that survives the drive itself.

That drive can weaken for reasons that aren’t really my fault. I can get old, sick, depressed, or grieving, and I would hope the agape is deep enough that she sticks by me through some of that even if it puts strain on eros. But if I just get bored with life, stop having much of a life outside her, and make her responsible for nearly all my warmth, meaning, reassurance, and excitement, that’s different. When I’m in love, my partner is my everything. Everything else drops away. I still try to make some time for friends, but really all I want to do is be with her.

Part of why it feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who’s fully got your back. You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance. But keep some room to explore life on your own.

This section will be relevant to some readers and easy for others to skip.

Before I say anything good about psychedelics for relationships, the warning has to come first. I don’t think sexual consent should be negotiated for the first time while high. The drug is changing how safe, loving, open, and connected everything feels. Advance planning doesn’t turn getting high and starting a relationship into a safe procedure. People need that warning before they take it, because once you’re inside that feeling, sober caveats may sound ridiculous.

Starting a relationship through psychedelics has another danger. Key and I met and then spent a few days taking iboga with friends. We got to know each other very deeply that way, and that was great. But it was especially her higher self I was getting to know. I tend to idealize people even sober, and that gets worse when I’m high. It was still beautiful to see the real higher self potential in her, I’m not denying that. But that information didn’t help me understand how we would get along in normal life.

I’ve also had friends get together at MDMA parties and stuff. It’s rarely a good idea. The intimacy can be completely real without telling you whether the two of you actually work together sober. Or you might even sometimes have the opposite problem, like I had with H., where the connection continues to deepen while sober, and it becomes something that one person might cling to desperately, never imagining they could find that again.

The obvious advice is to wait before making large promises and spend time together sober, around other people, and in ordinary situations. Write down what each of you learned, do some peer counseling, check with friends to see if you’re too pie-in-the-sky. But the problem is, you won’t necessarily be interested in sober advice when you’re high. You’re “beyond all that.” And the high can continue after sobriety because intimacy itself is like rose-colored glasses.

text:
Romantic love is not easy, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can’t sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!)

A relationship like this is rare, and that’s probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history. One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with Key: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They’re suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we can’t imagine prior. Nobody can command the spirit to remain. At our best, we serve it and listen for what Spirit wants to change. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn’t have articulated that since I didn’t even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But pathology festers when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture hermetically seals two people together and calls that a luxurious privacy. It tells them that sealed room should provide all the fresh air you’d get from a lover, family, community, therapist, and so on. Then it treats the predictable failure as privately caused as well, like mold that grows out of nowhere.

text:
Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” would make for a pretty weird date.

At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”

“I have baggage” isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now. What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.

Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them. What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward? text:
English isn’t a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don’t have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love, and so forth. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, “May all beings be at ease, pure of heart, and free.” It’s not about them being yours.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): "I want us to be special to each other, with our lives entangled. I want us to pay a lot of attention to each other and to desire each other sexually." I don’t think there’s anything fake or shameful about this.

A good relationship must have both kinds of love at once. Too often, the trouble is there’s a whole lot of I want you and hardly any I want you to be happy.

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else? The first reaction is horror, but if they can get past it, wanting her and wanting her to be happy stop fighting each other. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone, so if she’d be happier with somebody else, I’d want her less anyway.

text:
It’s hard to find sexually monogamous animals; have you ever looked? And as it turns out, we humans aren’t a natural exception to the rule, either. Plenty of tribal cultures were (and some still are) much looser about this, while still generally retaining the primary-partner “social monogamy.” Sexclusivity started gaining sway around the time we started planting crops and owning land. That’s when it made sense to keep track of how to keep our land in the family bloodline.

Ironically, sexclusivity, which we treat as the basis of romance, started out as that kind of bureaucratic record-keeping. By the 17th century, when England began mass urbanization by forcing peasants off their land, it became the legal definition of marriage. As for what comes naturally to us underneath that law, I’m not trying to say we’re just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity.

text:
This section will be relevant to some readers and easy for others to skip.

I’m putting the warning before anything good I say about psychedelics for relationships, because people need to hear it before they take anything. I don’t think sexual consent should be negotiated for the first time while high, when the drug is changing how safe, loving, open, and connected everything feels. And even if the two of you plan it all in advance, getting high and starting a relationship is still a risk.

Starting a relationship through psychedelics has another danger. Key and I met and then spent a few days taking iboga with friends. We got to know each other very deeply that way, and that was great. But it was especially her higher self I was getting to know. I tend to idealize people even sober, and that gets worse when I’m high. It was still beautiful to see the real higher self potential in her, I’m not denying that. But that information didn’t help me understand how we would get along in normal life.

I’ve also had friends get together at MDMA parties and stuff. It’s rarely a good idea. The intimacy can be completely real without telling you whether the two of you actually work together sober. Or you might even sometimes have the opposite problem, like I had with H., where the connection continues to deepen while sober, and it becomes something that one person might cling to desperately, never imagining they could find that again.

The obvious advice is to wait before making large promises and spend time together sober, around other people, and in ordinary situations. Write down what each of you learned, do some peer counseling, check with friends to see if you’re too pie-in-the-sky. But the problem is, you won’t necessarily be interested in sober advice when you’re high. You’re “beyond all that.” And the high can continue after sobriety because intimacy itself is like rose-colored glasses.

text:
Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, Ann, to two counselors. The male counselor eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There’s no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it fairly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.

I can believe a friend’s experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. I lived all the permutations of this with Bee, except that we never lived in community. I suspect if we had, we might still be together. She would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. And it’s actually natural to be a bit BPD when your entire survival depends on one person, because if they aren’t perfect, and especially if you need a lot of support, how will you survive? One fairly normal but large flaw in them could make your life really difficult. We were left alone inside something that needed other people around it, and that’s what’s happening to most people these days.

With H., I learned another part of the same dyad problem: not to treat what either of us thought the relationship was as a guarantee of what it would remain, because feelings can and usually do change over time. In our case, the relationship continued to naturally deepen while our outside relationships often felt more shallow, so it was natural for the dependency to increase. She was never into monogamy, but that didn’t stop her from becoming possessive once she found someone really worth keeping. And then she began demonizing me when I refused to be possessed. Because we did not have a shared community capable of supporting us, her friends heard her side and affirmed her truth.

So if you don’t have a real community already, what can you do about it practically, right now?

Make as much community as you can wherever you are, like going to Meetups together and making deep friendships as a couple. Find some shared purpose beyond maintaining the relationship. Introduce your old friends to your partner and try to mutualize those friendships as much as possible, so they aren’t experienced as slyly antagonistic or partial to one side. You don’t need to spend all your time together, but two completely separate social worlds will automatically start taking sides when something goes wrong.

text:
Conventional marriage vows are dishonest and inept, and most people know it. You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future, but you can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up emotionally, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do even if your feelings change. More importantly, though, if you do keep those promises, it's quite likely that your connection will deepen, so it's not like we truly have no control of future feelings, but just not completely, directly or unilaterally.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it, and that if you then tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, God will be angry and destroy your work.

Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage. That trend has continued evolving like a snowball until today. But what our ancestors knew was not wrong: You can sign a contract about what you’ll do, but feelings aren’t contractual.

text:
Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” would make for a pretty weird date.

At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”

“I have baggage” isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now. What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how well we actually handle our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.

Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them. What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward? Not doing can be just as bad as overdoing. If conflict makes you shut down, does it mean you stop talking to your partner for days, leaving them feeling abandoned?

Has your judgment gotten better, or would your friends or exes say you keep falling for the same stuff?

text:
Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.

Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends anymore. That’s a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. If one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system for housing, money, children, health, and emotional crises, so who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support, but I think that’s rare. Often, a friend who actually knows us both sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, if both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.

Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. They’re helpful when you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.

If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. They’re only hearing your side, usually while you’re upset, and they may just be trying to protect you, so take what they say with a grain of salt.

text:
I lived all the permutations of this with Bee, except that we never lived in community. I suspect if we had, we might still be together. She would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. Baseless accusations only work with friends who only know one side.

Commune friends could also have helped her in ways I couldn’t, because she was projecting onto me, which made me the wrong person to help her see beyond the projection. And it’s actually natural to be a bit BPD when your entire survival depends on one person, because if they aren’t perfect, and especially if you need a lot of support, how will you survive? One fairly normal but large flaw in them could make your life really difficult. We were left alone inside something that needed other people around it, and that’s what’s happening to most people these days.

H. taught me another part of the same dyad problem. I learned not to treat what either of us thought the relationship was as a guarantee of what it would remain, because feelings can and usually do change over time. In our case, the relationship continued to naturally deepen while our outside relationships often felt more shallow, so it was natural for the dependency to increase. She was never into monogamy, but that didn’t stop her from becoming possessive once she found someone really worth keeping. And then she began demonizing me when I refused to be possessed. Because we did not have a shared community capable of supporting us, her friends heard her side and affirmed her truth. The accusations couldn’t have survived among people who knew us both.

So if you don’t have a real community already, what can you do about it practically, right now?

Make as much community as you can wherever you are, like going to Meetups together and making deep friendships as a couple. Find some shared purpose beyond maintaining the relationship. Introduce your old friends to your partner and try to mutualize those friendships as much as possible, so they aren’t experienced as slyly antagonistic or partial to one side. You don’t need to spend all your time together, but two completely separate social worlds will automatically start taking sides when something goes wrong.

Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.

Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends anymore. That’s a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. If one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system for housing, money, children, health, and emotional crises. Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support, but I think that’s rare. Often, a friend who actually knows us both sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, If both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.

Separate confidants help when you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.

If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you, because they’re only hearing your side, usually while you’re upset, and they may just be trying to protect you.

text:
Even if I found my twin flame, she’d still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we’d still need other people around us.

Here’s how this looks for me: whenever something serious comes up in my relationships, we each run to our own friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends anymore. That’s a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. If one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system, covering the housing and the money, looking after the children and handling whatever health or emotional crisis comes up, so who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support, but I think that’s rare, because it’s often a friend who actually knows us both who sees the dysfunctional pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, if both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.

Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling, but if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner, so neither way is perfect.

If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. Take what they say with a grain of salt, since they’re only hearing your side, usually while you’re upset, and they may just be trying to protect you.
